title: How the Stage Was Set
framing: This prologue lists, in sourced steps, how oversight offices, ethics rules, the Justice Department and the clemency process changed around Trump before and during the acts this count records. It places those steps beside the acts without claiming that any one step caused any particular act, and its last section describes limits in the law rather than steps he took.
method: Seven themed finders read the Trump Tracker corpus and the corruption ledger; a verifier per theme checked every beat against its entry (facts, verbatim sources, dates); a synthesis wrote the outline; a critic checked it against the reader’s four examples and for overreach; one gap-fill round added four entries. Every URL below appears in a tracker entry or the ledger; the gate ran after the sweep with zero misses.

sections.title: Removing the watchdogs
sections.thesis: After inspectors general examining two Cabinet members were removed in 2020, the second term removed roughly 17 inspectors general and the head of the ethics office within weeks, later stripped whistleblower appeal rights from about 50,000 workers, and won a ruling that the president may fire an FTC member without cause.

beats.line: In May 2020, Trump told Congress that State Department inspector general Steve Linick was out while Linick examined Pompeo's use of staff; the next day the acting Transportation inspector general, whose office was investigating Chao, was replaced.
beats.why: The ledger labels it obstruction of oversight and notes that successors later completed both investigations.
beats.entryTitle: Trump removes the inspectors general investigating Pompeo and Chao

sources.text: NPR: President Trump Fires State Department Inspector General Steve Linick
Politico: Trump ousts State Department watchdog
Politico: Democrats blast removal of acting DOT inspector general

beats.line: In October 2020, Trump signed Executive Order 13957 creating Schedule F, which would have stripped job protections from tens of thousands of federal employees; Biden revoked it in January 2021.
beats.why: The entry says Trump vowed to reinstate it immediately if re-elected.
beats.entryTitle: Schedule F created in 2020 to strip civil service protections

sources.text: Trump White House Archives: Executive Order on Creating Schedule F In The Excepted Service
GAO: Civil Service: Agency Responses and Perspectives on Former Executive Order
White House (2025): Restoring Accountability To Policy-Influencing Positions

beats.line: On January 24, 2025, the administration removed the inspectors general of roughly 17 agencies without the 30 days' notice and case-specific reasons the law requires.
beats.why: The ledger says the purge cleared out the offices that had produced the first term's findings on Price, Pruitt, Zinke, Shulkin and Chao.
beats.entryTitle: Trump fires about 17 inspectors general in one Friday night

sources.text: NPR: Trump fires independent inspectors general at several agencies

beats.line: On February 10, 2025, three weeks into the term, Trump ousted David Huitema, the Senate-confirmed head of the Office of Government Ethics.
beats.why: The office certifies executive-branch financial disclosures and refused to certify Wilbur Ross's in the first term; the ledger files the removal under dismantling enforcement.
beats.entryTitle: Trump removes the director of the Office of Government Ethics

sources.text: CBS News: Trump ousts director of Office of Government Ethics

beats.line: Around March 8, 2026, the Schedule Policy/Career rule took effect, converting about 50,000 policy-influencing federal employees into at-will workers who lose Merit Systems Protection Board appeal rights and access to the whistleblower process.
beats.why: The entry's own reading is that workers who report fraud, waste or illegal activity can now be fired for it with no legal recourse.
beats.entryTitle: Schedule F takes effect and strips whistleblower process from about 50,000 workers

beats.line: The New York Times reported that senior CFTC officials sidelined career staff who raised concerns about three firms tied to Trump family members, and that two officials who had raised questions were placed on leave and put under internal investigation.
beats.why: Each firm needed CFTC sign-off for its prediction-market plans; per the Times account, the acting chair and her senior counsel intervened on each.
beats.entryTitle: CFTC sidelined staff who questioned Trump-tied crypto firms, NYT reports

beats.line: On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the president may fire an FTC member without cause, overruling the 1935 Humphrey's Executor precedent.
beats.why: The entry reads the logic as reaching the NLRB, Merit Systems Protection Board and Consumer Product Safety Commission; the Federal Reserve was excepted.
beats.quote: Subordinates who exercise the President's power are subject to removal by him.
beats.entryTitle: Supreme Court lets Trump fire independent-agency members at will

sections.title: Loosening the ethics rules
sections.thesis: Trump kept his businesses in a revocable trust under a company ethics plan with no ban on new foreign private deals, a first-day order revoked the appointee ethics pledge order, and later steps paused new foreign-bribery enforcement, ended shell-company ownership reporting and withdrew the United States from Europe's anti-corruption monitor.

beats.line: The Trump Organization's second-term ethics plan put the businesses in a trust run by Trump's children and barred new deals with foreign governments but, unlike the 2017 plan, placed no ban on new foreign private deals.
beats.why: CNN noted the pledge was silent on how the company would handle overseas business deals.
beats.quote: The ethics pledge, however, is silent on how the company will handle overseas business deals
beats.entryTitle: The second-term ethics plan allows new foreign private deals

beats.line: Trump took office in January 2025 without selling his assets or placing them in a qualified blind trust; they sit in a revocable trust overseen by Donald Trump Jr. that Trump can amend or revoke.
beats.why: In its own analysis, the ledger calls this arrangement the precondition for the deals, token sales and licensing fees it records.
beats.entryTitle: Trump took office without divesting or a blind trust

beats.line: On August 11, 2026, FinCEN issued a final rule permanently ending the requirement that U.S. companies report their beneficial owners, and said it will delete ownership information already filed by U.S. persons now exempt.
beats.why: Per the entry, the requirement was meant to make anonymous shell companies harder to use; deleting records means a later administration cannot simply reinstate them.

beats.why: GRECO's 2023 evaluation noted the president and vice president are exempt from most conflict-of-interest rules; the Council says GRECO remains open to resuming cooperation.

sections.title: Enforcement cut back and clemency routed around the pardon office

beats.line: The New York Times reported that Trump allies collected tens of thousands of dollars from felons seeking clemency, and the Washington Post found about 100 of Trump's 237 clemency grants went to people who never petitioned the pardon office.
beats.why: A first-term precedent: per these reports, connections rather than the Justice Department process were one route to clemency.

sections.title: The law's limits around a sitting president
sections.thesis: These are limits in the law, not acts the tracker attributes to Trump: trading, anti-bribery and emoluments rules apply to a sitting president but lack enforcement absent Justice Department action, presidents are not subject to the ethics laws barring conflicts for most executive employees, last year's stablecoin law did not extend to Trump or his family, and a House-passed ban on members buying stocks stalled in a party-line Senate fight over voter ID.

beats.line: OGE published Trump's first-quarter 2026 disclosure on May 14, 2026, showing more than 3,700 trades in three months, including Nvidia, Palantir and Axon purchases that NOTUS reported coincided with administration actions boosting those companies' business.
beats.why: Per the entry, the STOCK Act, anti-bribery statutes and Domestic Emoluments Clause apply but lack enforcement against a sitting president absent Justice Department action.
beats.entryTitle: More than 3,700 trades in a quarter, and no enforcement route against a sitting president

gaps: Stock trading (the reader's second example) holds only in part. No entry or ledger item shows Trump pushing to keep Congress from banning stock trading. The corpus records only H.R. 7008 stalling in the Senate on a 53-47 party-line cloture vote over a voter-ID attachment, so the prologue presents it as a limit in the law, not as a step he took. The prologue should not promise readers the claim as the reader framed it.

Inspectors general: the inspectors-general-purge entry ('17+ on first day', January 20, 2025) has the date wrong, so the outline uses the ledger item (January 24, 2025, roughly 17 agencies, NPR). The Social Security IG entry says 19. Print only 'roughly 17'.
Loyalists and the personal attorney as attorney general are both supported: Patel, Bondi, Blanche, Halligan, Pulte, Rogoff and the OPM question.
Removal of the Office of Special Counsel head and the FEC's lost quorum: no tracker entry exists, so neither is used.

Public Integrity Section 36-to-two figure: the CR-15 entry states it and attributes it to NOTUS, but none of the beat's three listed sources is a NOTUS piece. A NOTUS source needs to be added before publishing. The AP's 'expected' cut to five lawyers was taken out of the FCPA beat's line.
Blanche's 50-49 confirmation is sourced here to the Washington Post. The Senate roll call (vote 230), which the Blanche campaign-rallies entry cites, could be added as a primary source.
CFTC: the critic's figure (2 crypto enforcement cases this term against more than 80 under Biden) is not in the verified beat, so it is not used.
Musk's exemption from public financial disclosure was left out. Its why was defective, and its $300 billion contracts figure rests on generic, non-article sources.

The clemency half of the enforcement section rests on one tracker entry (pardon brokers) plus two ledger items. The rules section rests on two tracker entries (FinCEN, GRECO) plus four ledger items. Every section has at least two sourced items.

Left out as outside the setup theme or the corruption scope: the ICE detention ombudsman closure (a civil-rights complaint office whose closure is in dispute), the Gabbard referral against a 2020 IG, the Massie/Cassidy/Paxton primaries, the NLRB and EAC quorum losses, and the ballroom and pardon acts themselves, which belong in the count.

The Bloomberg trade-count beat is listed as 2026-08-22 but describes the September 15 analysis, so it is dated 2026-09-15. The H.R. 7008 beat is listed as 2026-03-26 but describes the September 30 vote, so it is dated 2026-09-30. Placeholder dates: the Patel beat (2025-01-20) and the cabinet-dissenter beat (2017-01-20) carry start-of-term dates. Neither entry gives an appointment or removal date, and the dissenter events fall in 2018 to 2020. Do not present either as an event date.

Inferred theses: the loyalists thesis says the entry 'ties' the first-term removals to loyalty, but only AP on Esper states a loyalty motive, and PolitiFact supports the pace of the removals, not their reasons. The limits thesis is composed from four entries; its claim that these are not acts attributed to Trump rests on no entry assigning them to him.

Inferred or attributed whys: Bondi appointment (restates the entry's sequence and alleges no exchange); Bondi firing (reasons come from reporting); first-term clemency precedent (a reading of the NYT and Post reports); ethics-pledge and FCPA beats (the ledger's 'dismantling enforcement' label); revocable trust (the ledger's own analysis that it is a precondition, not a finding); Schedule Policy/Career ('no legal recourse' is the entry's reading); OLC opinion (the entry's analysis); Slaughter (the reach beyond the FTC is the entry's reading); Rogoff (the entry's view); pardon brokers (the entry's view that sidelining created the market); FinCEN (the entry's statement of purpose and effect).

Alleged or disputed: CFTC staff sidelining comes from the New York Times and is relayed by secondhand outlets, one headlined 'alleges'. That the intervention followed staff concerns is implied, not stated. Oyer's firing and its reason are her own account. The 2024 bribery probe being 'dead' is reported only by ProPublica. The state bar rule is a proposal, and the McDade conflict is the critics' view. Pardon brokers' claims are their own, and no pardon-for-payment is established. The NOTUS trade timing shows coincidence, not trading on inside information. The OPM ruling is preliminary, and politicization is the unions' argument. Halligan's dismissals were without prejudice.

GRECO: the tracker attributes the presidential-exemption finding to the Guardian. The Council of Europe says GRECO remains open to resuming cooperation, so do not describe the outside review as ended.

Trump Organization plan: the outline does not link the plan's missing ban on new foreign private deals to CREW's count of 23 foreign projects. Some of those projects involve government-linked developers, which the plan nominally barred.
The $2.16 billion disclosure figure includes gross business revenue, not profit. It is the tracker's own sum of the form's exact amounts.
Blanche crypto transfer: 'technically legal but at odds with its spirit' is what experts told ProPublica. The department and Blanche's own characterizations are not in the beat.
Kash Patel beat: 'Over my dead body' is Bill Barr's first-term remark and must stay attributed to him.

critic.verdict: The outline covers three of the reader's four examples with real entries: the inspectors general (through the ledger, which is better than the defective inspectors-general-purge entry), loyalists, and Blanche as attorney general. The fourth holds only in part. The corpus documents the H.R. 7008 stall, but no entry or ledger item shows Trump pressing against a stock-trading ban. The outline's gap note on this is correct and should be kept. The biggest omission among setup acts already in the corpus is blanche-disbands-doj-crypto-enforcement-team-while-holding-crypto. It is a Blanche memo that disbanded the DOJ crypto unit while he held crypto, so it joins the reader's personal-attorney and dismantled-enforcement themes in one sourced beat. bondi-doj-block-ethics-investigations (the state-bar rule) is also missing. The Foreign Influence Task Force and FARA memo was dropped for a date problem that is easy to fix (February 5, 2025). Missing too is cftc-purged-staff-trump-crypto-firms-nyt (2 crypto enforcement cases this term against more than 80 under Biden). Neither the OSC head's removal nor the FEC's lost quorum has any entry, so neither can be used. Two of the outline's gap notes are factually wrong. The NOTUS figure (Public Integrity Section down from 36 corruption lawyers to two) is sourced in the CR-15 entry and can replace the AP's 'expected' cut. Blanche's 50-49 confirmation has a primary source (Senate roll call 230) in the Blanche campaign-rallies entry. Also, the Bloomberg trade-count beat is dated 2026-08-22 but describes the September 15 analysis, a date mismatch the cautions do not list. On overreach, the most serious problem is the congress thesis saying trading rules 'do not reach' a sitting president; its own basis entry says they apply but go unenforced without DOJ action. Next is the congress section's framing, which implies Trump designed a stall the entry attributes to a Senate voter-ID fight. Also overstated: the Massie beat (outside the thesis and outside the corruption scope), the Slaughter generalization without the Fed exception, and the ombudsman and Gabbard beats as 'watchdogs'. With those fixes and the additions, the prologue is sound and sourced, but it should not promise readers the stock-trading claim as framed.
overreach: Congress thesis says 'existing trading and stablecoin rules do not reach a sitting president'. The basis entry (trump-q1-2026-disclosure-3700-trades-nvidia-palantir-axon) says the STOCK Act, anti-bribery statutes and the Domestic Emoluments Clause 'all apply but have no enforcement mechanism against a sitting president without DOJ action'. Only the stablecoin-law half (AP: it 'did not extend to Trump or his family') is supported. Rewrite the trading half as 'apply but are not enforced against a sitting president without Justice Department action'.

Congress section as a whole: the stock-ban beat records a party-line Senate fight over a voter-ID attachment. Placing it in a prologue of Trump's setup steps implies he caused the stall, and no entry says so. The framing disclaimer does not cure a section title ('What Congress left open') that reads as part of his design.

Massie/Cassidy/Paxton beat: the congress thesis does not mention it, and its link to corruption setup rests only on the entry's own inference ('the price of opposing Trump... demonstrated twice'). One listed source (Politico on ballroom funding) supports a fact the line does not use, and the Esquire Paxton source is omitted. Cut it or move it, and attribute the 'price' framing.

Watchdogs thesis says the Supreme Court 'let the president fire independent-agency members at will'. The holding was about an FTC member. The reach to the NLRB, MSPB and CPSC is the entry's and the coverage's reading of the logic, and the thesis drops the Federal Reserve exception the entry states. The thesis also says 'the inspectors general' as if all were removed; the basis says roughly 17.

Watchdogs section: the ICE detention ombudsman (a civil-rights complaint office) and the Gabbard referral (a 2026 criminal referral against an IG fired in 2020) do not watch for corruption, and neither appears in the 'removed the watchdogs who flagged first-term conduct' logic. Listing the ombudsman closure as a removal also takes a side in a dispute: DHS says Congress defunded it, while HuffPost reports the bill does not require closure.

Trump Organization beat why ('It left room for new foreign private deals; by May 2026 CREW counted 23 Trump-branded projects') implies the 23 projects flow from the plan's gap. The ledger only places the two facts side by side, and some of those projects involve government-linked developers such as Qatari Diar and Dar Global, which the plan nominally barred.
GRECO why ('leaving ends that outside review for now') is an inference. The entry quotes the Council of Europe saying GRECO 'remains open to resuming cooperation'.

Bondi-fired beat why ('in charge of the department that decides cases touching Trump') and Patel/Bondi/Blanche appointment whys are the outline's own characterizations, not entry statements. The outline flags them; they still need hedged wording.

OLC beat why ('matters most if Democrats win the House'), Schedule Policy/Career why ('fired for it with no legal recourse'), Habba why ('second workaround') and pardon-broker why ('market exists because the process was sidelined') are the entries' own analysis. They must be attributed, not stated as findings.

Revocable-trust beat why repeats the ledger's 'precondition for the deals... that follow'. That is an analytic claim of enablement, the very connection the framing says the prologue does not make. Attribute it or soften it.
